titulo: Why Fermat's method sometimes takes longer

frases: Why can we factor some numbers almost instantly, while others take many attempts?
Thirty-five is five times seven, two factors that are close together.
Six squared minus thirty-five equals one. The method works immediately.
Now take two hundred and thirteen, equal to three times seventy-one.
Its square root lies between fourteen and fifteen, so we start with fifteen.
Fifteen squared minus two hundred and thirteen equals twelve, not a perfect square.
With sixteen, we get forty-three. So we keep searching.
At thirty-seven, the difference is finally another perfect square.
Thirty-seven minus thirty-four equals three, and their sum is seventy-one.
When factors are close, Fermat's method can be very fast.
When they are far apart, the search can become much longer.
This illustrates one limitation, but does not explain every aspect of RSA security.
Modern factoring algorithms use much more sophisticated mathematical techniques.
In the lab, we can measure those attempts and discover where each algorithm works.
Every explanation comes with code, tests and reproducible results.
